statement: Prime numbers are more than any assigned multitude of prime numbers.
heath_proof: Let A, B, C be the assigned prime numbers; I say that there are more prime numbers than A, B, C. For let the least number measured by A, B, C be taken, and let it be DE; let the unit DF be added to DE. Then EF is either prime or not. First, let it be prime; then the prime numbers A, B, C, EF have been found which are more than A, B, C. Next, let EF not be prime; therefore it is measured by some prime number. [VII. 31] Let it be measured by the prime number G. I say that G is not the same with any of the numbers A, B, C. For, if possible, let it be so. Now A, B, C measure DE; therefore G also will measure DE. But it also measures EF. Therefore G, being a number, will measure the remainder, the unit DF: which is absurd. Therefore G is not the same with any one of the numbers A, B, C. And by hypothesis it is prime. Therefore the prime numbers A, B, C, G have been found which are more than the assigned multitude of A, B, C.
ai_proof_text:
9.20
**Statement:** Prime numbers are more than any assigned multitude of prime numbers.

**Step 1.** Let A, B, C be any assigned multitude of prime numbers. We shall show that there exists a prime number beyond those assigned.

**Step 2.** Let DE be the least number measured by A, B, and C. Such a number exists: for instance, the product A times B times C is measured by each of A, B, and C, by the definition of multiplication [D7.15] and measurement [D7.3]. (We may take DE to be this product, or any common multiple; the argument requires only that A, B, and C each measure DE.)

**Step 3.** Add a unit to DE, and let EF equal one unit, so that DF = DE + 1.

**Step 4.** Now DF is either prime or composite [D7.11, D7.13].

**Step 5.** Case 1: Suppose DF is prime. Since DF = DE + 1 and DE is measured by each of A, B, C, we have DF > A, DF > B, and DF > C (because DE is at least as large as each prime factor, and DF = DE + 1). Thus DF is a prime number different from each of A, B, and C.

**Step 6.** Case 2: Suppose DF is composite. Then by Proposition 7.31, some prime number G measures DF.

**Step 7.** We claim that G is not equal to any of A, B, or C. For suppose, toward a contradiction, that G is one of A, B, C — say G equals A.

**Step 8.** Now A measures DE (by construction in Step 2). And A (being equal to G) measures DF (by Step 6). Since A measures both DF and DE, and DF = DE + EF where EF is a unit, A must also measure the remainder EF, which is a unit. (For if a number measures a whole and a part taken from it, it measures the remainder as well, which follows from the nature of measurement [D7.3, D5.1].)

**Step 9.** But A is a prime number, and hence is greater than a unit [D7.11, D7.1]. A number greater than a unit cannot measure a unit, since the only number that measures a unit is the unit itself. This is a contradiction.

**Step 10.** Therefore G is not equal to A. By the same reasoning, G is not equal to B, and G is not equal to C. Hence G is a prime number different from all of A, B, and C.

**Step 11.** In either case (whether DF is prime or composite), we have found a prime number — either DF itself or G — that is not among the originally assigned primes A, B, and C.

**Step 12.** Since A, B, C were any assigned multitude of prime numbers, this shows that for any finite collection of primes, there exists a prime not in that collection. Therefore, prime numbers are more than any assigned multitude of prime numbers. Q.E.D.
